query: W is attractive for plasma-facing divertor components because of its high melting point, thermal resistance, low sputtering yield, and low tritium retention, but its relatively high ductile-to-brittle transition temperature limits use. CuCrZr provides favorable thermal conductivity as a heat sink but has a narrow operating-temperature range and is susceptible to irradiation embrittlement, requiring an intermediate layer that transfers heat efficiently while keeping both materials within suitable temperature ranges. Earlier HEA studies reported elevated-temperature strength retention in MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW, thermal stability in Mo6.6Nb6Ni80Ta1.4Ti6, and favorable combinations of strength and ductility in NbTaTiV, HfNbTaTiZr, and TiVNbTa. Nevertheless, HEA performance can involve tradeoffs among strength, ductility, thermal stability, and phase constitution. TiVNbTa in a single-phase BCC dendritic state combines about 800 MPa yield strength with approximately 40% strain, but its reported yield and compressive strengths at 1273 K are only 330 and 423 MPa, respectively, at 30% strain. Under the constraints of efficient W-to-CuCrZr heat transfer, high-temperature mechanical stability, and compatibility with the limited operating ranges of both adjoining materials, what single intervention could improve the TiVNbTa intermediate material? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, causal mechanism, predicted change relative to the reported TiVNbTa baseline, temperature and loading boundaries, supporting evidence from the prior HEA results, and a controlled experiment that would falsify both the performance prediction and the proposed mechanism.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a modest tungsten addition to the TiVNbTa high-entropy alloy (HEA) to form a TiVNbTaW alloy will improve its high‐temperature mechanical stability while retaining its room‐temperature ductility and maintaining adequate thermal transfer between the W plasma‐facing component and the CuCrZr heat sink.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase BCC TiVNbTa alloy showing ~800 MPa yield strength at room temperature but reduced yield and compressive strengths (330 MPa and 423 MPa, respectively) at 1273 K.
generation.intervention: Alloy modification by adding tungsten at a modest concentration (for example, on the order of 5–10 at.%), effectively transforming TiVNbTa into TiVNbTaW.
generation.conditions: High-temperature environment (around 1273 K) under compressive loading, representative of the operating conditions for plasma-facing divertor interlayer applications with adjacent W and CuCrZr components.
generation.structural_mediator: Increased lattice distortion and solid-solution strengthening induced by tungsten incorporation while preserving the BCC phase; also, tungsten’s high melting point promotes thermal stability.
generation.mechanism: W acts by providing solid-solution strengthening and enhanced dislocation resistance at elevated temperatures. Its inherently high melting point and compatibility with the plasma-facing W component help retain mechanical strength and stability at 1273 K, thus reducing the reduction in load-bearing capacity observed in pure TiVNbTa.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in high-temperature yield and compressive strengths relative to the reported values of TiVNbTa (i.e. improvements beyond 330 MPa yield strength at 1273 K) without significant loss of ductility, while still ensuring efficient W-to-CuCrZr heat transfer.
generation.baseline: TiVNbTa single-phase HEA with ~800 MPa yield strength at room temperature and reduced performance (~330 MPa yield strength at 1273 K) under high-temperature compressive loading.
generation.boundary: The improvement is expected primarily in the temperature range around 1273 K under compressive loads; however, an excessive tungsten addition could lead to the formation of brittle secondary phases and/or degrade room-temperature ductility and thermal conductivity.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal tungsten content for balancing high-temperature strength, ductility, and thermal conduction is not precisely established, and quantitative gains in mechanical properties remain to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of consolidated HEA samples with nominal compositions of TiVNbTa and with incremental tungsten additions (e.g., 0, 5, and 10 at.% W) via spark plasma sintering. Conduct comprehensive high-temperature (around 1273 K) compressive mechanical tests, along with phase analysis (XRD) and thermal conductivity measurements under conditions replicating the W-to-CuCrZr interface.
measurements: Strain to failure (ductility) at high temperature
Thermal conductivity across the temperature range
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the tungsten-alloyed samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in high-temperature mechanical strength relative to pure TiVNbTa, or if detrimental phase changes occur (e.g., formation of brittle secondary phases) or if there is a significant degradation in thermal conductivity or ductility, then the hypothesis is falsified.

The International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor aims to study the feasibility of tokamak-type reactors and test technologies and materials for commercial use. One major challenge is developing materials for the reactor’s divertor, which supports high thermal flux. Tungsten was chosen as the plasma-facing material, while a CuCrZr alloy will be used in the cooling pipes. However, the gradient between the working temperatures of these materials requires the use of a thermal barrier interlayer between them. To this end, refractory high-entropy (CrFeTiTa)70W30 and VFeTiTaW alloys were prepared by mechanical alloying and sintering, and their thermal and irradiation resistance was evaluated. Both alloys showed phase growth after annealing at 1100 °C for 8 days, being more pronounced for higher temperatures (1300 °C and 1500 °C). The VFeTiTaW alloy presented greater phase growth, suggesting lower microstructural stability, however, no new phases were formed. In this study, bulk samples of a CrMoNbWV high-entropy alloy (HEA) were obtained for the first time by spark plasma sintering (SPS) of mechanically alloyed (MA) powders at 1200 °C, 1300 °C, and 1400 °C. Microstructure evolution, phase formation as well as wear and corrosion behavior were investigated. The MA powders’ phase composition was found to be represented by body-centered-cubic (BCC) solid solution. The solid solution partially decomposed to Laves phases under the sintering, such as Cr2Nb and (Fe, Cr)Nb, and NbVO4-VO oxides mixture. The temperature increase to 1400 °C led to a grain coarsening of the BCC phase and decreased the Laves phase content accompanied by precipitation at the grain boundaries. The sintered samples showed high hardness and compressive strength (2700–2800 MPa) at room temperature. The wear tests demonstrated excellent results in comparison to conventional wear-resistant composites. The obtained samples also exhibited high corrosion resistance under electrochemical tests in H2SO4 solution.
